GPT-6 Astra + MiniMax H3

Created the kinetic typography effect in Blender using Astra, then used the resulting video as a reference in MiniMax H3 to restyle it.

If you're curious, here's the MiniMax H3 prompt:
Restyle @[video1], the supplied grayscale kinetic typography animation, into a finished, vibrant 15-second 16:9 motion-design film. Use it as the sole reference for typography geometry, animation, composition, camera movement and editing. Replace the grayscale materials and lighting with the treatments below, and create original music and synchronized sound effects.

Preserve the six words exactly, in this order: BREAK / EVERY / RULE / CREATE / PURE / MAGIC. Keep each word in its original 2.5-second section, with its own recognizable font, letter shapes, cutouts and proportions. Inherit the reference's entrances, collisions, elastic deformation, secondary rebounds, connected folds, sliding slices, spiral paths, exits and camera impulses. Preserve the large ! ? + * # = > symbols, their trajectories, depth layers and foreground passes. Keep the central word legible when it resolves. Carry the source choreography through the final MAGIC pose.

Give the sequence bold, carefully separated colors, rich material detail, directional studio lighting, convincing contact shadows and controlled reflections. Each section has its own material identity within one energetic graphic world. Enhance the existing backgrounds with the assigned palette, subtle texture and depth. Use restrained highlight bloom and directional motion blur on fast travel while keeping the resolved letter edges crisp. Preserve the source framing and cut rhythm.

0-2.5s, BREAK: Distressed scarlet-red painted letters against a deep charcoal background. Bright acid-yellow exclamation marks and punctuation explode around the red word. Preserve the rough type contours and dimensional sides. Raking light catches the paint texture; the existing impacts receive brief lighting accents. Dry heavy impacts, a low bass punch and fast outward whooshes follow the assembly and recoil.

2.5-5s, EVERY: Glossy cobalt-blue rubber letters against a warm off-white field, with coral question marks and plus signs. Broad soft reflections travel across the stretching surfaces. Keep the rubber wave and bouncing symbols from the reference. Add tightly synchronized elastic boings, rubber snaps and airy swishes, integrated into the rhythm.

5-7.5s, RULE: Brushed metallic letter faces on dark graphite carriages, with signal-orange pistons and orange punctuation accents. Retain the font's distinctive geometric cutouts. Warm orange edge light separates the machinery from the textured graphite setting. Give the opposing block collisions sharp metallic clacks, short low thuds and small ricochet ticks.

7.5-10s, CREATE: Warm cream paper leaves with deep petrol-blue lettering, coral punctuation and a dark petrol backdrop. Fine paper fibers and grazing light reveal every connected crease. Preserve the opening, traveling refold and spring-back. Add crisp paper flicks, folding rustles and light percussive pops as the symbols leave the folds.

10-12.5s, PURE: Acid-yellow enamel backing strips with glossy black condensed letters and a restrained graphite surround. Preserve the three actual horizontal text slices, opposing slide directions, secondary register slip and clean realignment. Specular streaks slide across the enamel without hiding the seams. Use precise sliding swishes and satisfying mechanical clicks at each registration.

12.5-15s, MAGIC: A rich violet background, pearlescent letter faces with turquoise edge reflections, and luminous turquoise and violet punctuation. Keep the source's orbital slingshot and outward symbol recoil; subtle iridescence shifts with the existing motion. Add a rising spiral whoosh and bright crystalline ticks, ending with a short shimmering chime while MAGIC remains readable and the surrounding symbols continue their source motion.

Create one continuous original instrumental electronic breakbeat across all six sections: punchy kick and snare, rapid hi-hats, syncopated synth bass and compact rising accents. Match strong musical accents to the existing word changes and impacts. Keep the mix energetic and clean, with distinct foreground effects and stereo movement following the symbols. Resolve the music with a decisive final accent and a short chime tail within the 15-second ending. No vocals, spoken words or subtitles. Add no extra words, logos or watermarks.

image_model_prompts:
GPT-6 Astra + MiniMax H3

A workflow I've been experimenting with:

First, used GPT-6 Astra with Blender to create the base video as a simple 3D previs. Then took that video into MiniMax H3 and used a character reference + prompt to replace the placeholder object, populate the environment and transform the whole scene into a polished 2D anime sequence.

The useful part is that Blender already solves the camera path, timing, scale, blocking and environment geometry.

So instead of asking the video model to figure out everything from scratch, you give it a moving blueprint and let it focus on the character, animation and final look.

You can find the MiniMax H3 prompt below.

Used a premade model from sketchfab for this experiment: "Day 5. Final:The Western Saloon" (https://skfb.ly/6TOJT) by Olyona Kuznetsova is licensed under Creative Commons Attribution.

Seedance 2.5 Prompt:
@[image1] defines the Speedster’s complete appearance; treat the three turnaround views as one continuous person and ignore the neutral background.

A live-action superhero rescue unfolds with the playful suspended-time spectacle of the X-Men: Apocalypse mansion rescue. Every rescue follows one strict route: the Speedster takes each person directly from inside the mansion, crosses the front entrance, and places them in one safe gathering area beneath the large oak tree. He never leaves anyone in another interior room. Once rescued, every person remains visibly outside as the crowd grows.

0-3 seconds: Beneath the oak tree, the Speedster casually chats and laughs with a young woman while the mansion fills the background; a sudden orange explosion erupts through the lower windows behind them, reflected in his visor before either turns around.

3-4 seconds: He glances over his shoulder, gives the woman a calm “one moment” gesture, and launches toward the mansion as the world drops into extreme time dilation.

4-6 seconds: A low tracking shot follows him through the front entrance into a hallway of nearly frozen fire, airborne glass, dust, and suspended residents; cyan-white speed energy cuts through the orange blast.

6-8 seconds: He gathers two students before a ceiling beam reaches them, carries both through the front door, places them safely beside the woman under the oak, and reverses instantly.

8-10 seconds: He catches a falling teacher and a frightened student in the library, races them outside together, and sets both upright in the same gathering area as books hang motionless behind him.

10-12 seconds: Crossing the kitchen, he notices a fresh pizza suspended above a table, casually takes one slice and bites it while using his free arm to carry the cook directly outside; the remaining pizza stays on the table.

12-14 seconds: He reaches an elderly man seated in his own wheelchair, grips the wheelchair frame, and transports the man and wheelchair together through the front entrance, parking both safely on the grass. The elderly man never leaves his wheelchair. No shopping cart appears.

14-16 seconds: He returns for a child and guardian trapped beside a cracking staircase, carries both outside in one pass, and gently places them together with the rescued crowd.

16-18 seconds: In the music room, he catches a violinist before a collapsing cabinet strikes, carries the violinist outside, then makes an immediate separate pass to save the violin case as a humorous afterthought.

18-20 seconds: Two residents are blown from an upper balcony; he races up the wall, intercepts both in the nearly frozen air, lands on the lawn, and places them safely beneath the oak.

20-22 seconds: A chandelier begins falling toward several students. He redirects it onto an empty marble floor, gathers the entire group, and completes several rapid doorway crossings until every student stands outside.

22-24 seconds: He carries a staff member and a small dog from a smoke-filled room, deposits both safely beside one another on the lawn, then returns the dog’s favorite cushion in a separate lightning-fast pass.

24-26 seconds: A compressed burst of very short cuts shows dozens of additional round trips through bedrooms, classrooms, bathrooms, and corridors. Every pass begins with the Speedster entering empty-handed and ends with different residents crossing the front threshold in his arms and joining the same outdoor crowd.

26-28 seconds: He performs a final high-speed sweep through visibly empty rooms, finds the last unconscious caretaker beneath a doorway, carries the caretaker outside, and clears the entrance one instant before the roof collapses.

28-30 seconds: Normal time returns as the mansion erupts behind the complete rescued crowd. The Speedster walks back to the young woman beneath the oak, resumes his original conversational posture, finishes the pizza slice, and smiles while she stares at him in stunned disbelief.

Use rapid 1-to-2-second kinetic cuts, whip pans, threshold match cuts, near-subject tracking, brief bullet-time inserts, and recurring exterior wides that clearly show the crowd accumulating. Preserve coherent mansion geography, the front-door-to-oak rescue axis, the advancing explosion, and every rescued person’s outdoor position. Keep only one physical Speedster; luminous trails may reveal repeated routes but never become duplicate bodies. Use photoreal cinematic detail, physically convincing weight, contact, cloth, fire, smoke, and debris. A playful retro-rock pulse accelerates through stretched glass chimes, rushing air, muffled impacts, and a full-volume final explosion. No intelligible dialogue and no subtitles.

I had a modest little short-form drama idea in mind, so I decided to make a 1.5 minute film with Seedance 2.5 and share the whole process.

First, without preparing any characters, environments or other references, I turned the entire idea into a story and squeezed it into a single 30 second prompt. I generated that version at 480p.

The goal here was simply to see how the characters, lighting, composition and overall visual direction would look and to check whether there were any logical problems or mistakes in the prompt.

As I mentioned before, if you give Seedance 2.5 more context than the duration can realistically handle, it tends to compensate by speeding up the scenes. As expected, most of the first version came out feeling fast-forwarded. After reviewing that video, I made a few more changes to the story.

Instead of creating the characters and the location from scratch, I decided to reuse what Seedance had already created in the first video.

I took screenshots from moments where the characters and environment were clearly visible, then used Seedream 5 Pro to create character sheets from them. For the restaurant, I removed the people from one of the frames and created a clean environment reference. For the charging booth, I generated an image in Midjourney and removed its background.

Then I revised the original prompt and split the story into three separate parts, creating three independent prompts.

The references I already had were enough for the first two parts. For the third part, realized I would also need a reference showing the restaurant at the end of the night with the curtains closed. So I grabbed another frame from the previous generation and added it as an environment reference for the third prompt.

I ran into one continuity issue in Part 3. In the final shot, the restaurant owner was walking outside in front of the restaurant, which broke the continuity.

Rather than regenerating the entire 30s sequence, I generated only that 10s specific shot with a new prompt. I cut the problematic section from the original version and replaced it with the new one.

At that point, the film was basically done. I added subtitles, upscaled it and finished the edit.

I didn't make this for a specific platform, publication or competition. It was mostly an experiment.

There are definitely things I could have done differently. I could have added voice references for the characters. I could have created another reference for the restaurant owner carrying her bag. I could also have prepared more angles of the restaurant and used those as environment references.

I wasn't completely happy with the closed-curtain version of the restaurant either, so that could have been prepared more carefully as a dedicated reference instead of relying on a frame from the generated video.

Overall, if you're thinking about making a 1 to 2 minute film, compressing the entire story into a 30-second test first can be a useful way to see whether the idea works visually.

Another useful method is taking frames from the footage you've already generated and using them as references for the next sections. It helps a lot with continuity without requiring you to design every single asset from scratch beforehand.

Including prompt revisions and generation time, the whole process took me a few hours. In total, I had to generate eight 30s clips and two 10s clips. One or two of those extra generations were mostly because I rushed a couple of things.

If you have any suggestions, ideas or techniques you use for this kind of workflow, I'd love to hear them.

I'm leaving the first test video below, along with the references I extracted and prepared from it, and the original prompt I used for that first generation.

Theme Based Collage Template

A flexible collage prompt for turning any theme into a series of connected visual moments. Change the parameters as you wish. Example values in the alts.

Prompt:
THEME = enter theme
STYLE = enter the style you want
PALETTE = enter the color palette
ASPECT RATIO = enter the aspect ratio you want

DO:
  Create an artistic multi-scene collage built entirely around THEME.
  Derive subjects, environments, objects, characters and visual events naturally from THEME.
  Derive the emotional tone, atmosphere and energy naturally from THEME.
  Use people, animals, objects, landscapes, architecture, abstract forms or any combination of them when they meaningfully support THEME.
  Treat each scene as a distinct emotional or conceptual fragment from the same world.
  Build the composition like an expressive editorial art spread rather than a storyboard or regular panel grid.
  Freely vary the number, scale, proportions and placement of scenes.
  Combine large dominant images with narrow vertical fragments, wide horizontal crops, small detail scenes and partially cropped compositions.
  Stagger scene edges and shift their alignments to create an irregular visual rhythm.
  Let some scenes extend fully to the canvas edge while others terminate against neighboring imagery.
  Use occasional L-shaped, stepped or offset arrangements created naturally by neighboring scene proportions.
  Avoid repeating the same rectangle size or alignment across the composition.
  Keep scenes visually separate without visible frames or empty gaps between them.
  Let neighboring scenes meet through irregular crop relationships while keeping their environments independent.
  Do not blend separate locations into one continuous environment.
  Keep the main subjects of each scene visually contained within that scene.
  Use architecture, large color fields and negative space to shape the overall composition.
  Connect neighboring scenes through color relationships, visual rhythm and thematic echoes rather than physically merging their content.
  Choose environments and situations specifically suited to THEME.
  Include occasional intimate fragments such as hands, objects, windows, silhouettes, architectural details or empty spaces when they strengthen THEME.
  Give each scene a different visual scale, point of view and conceptual focus.
  Use expressive lighting, shape, perspective and negative space according to STYLE.
  Vary the emphasis of PALETTE from scene to scene while preserving overall harmony.
  Maintain consistency whenever subjects, characters, objects or locations recur.
  Keep the final composition visually clean, sophisticated and intentionally irregular.

CAMERA: varied editorial framing, environmental wides, cropped medium views, isolated details, unusual negative-space compositions, overhead fragments and off-center perspectives chosen according to THEME

RULES:
  Use STYLE as the authority for medium, linework, texture, shading, shape design and overall rendering language.

P13: High front 3/4 FS, push: C2's heavy silver-blue sheet meets C1's upward split at contact 11, triggering pair 11; both load the overhead collision.

GPT Image 2 Prompt for storyboard:
Create a 16:9 clean monochrome 2D storyboard line-sketch sheet of Suzune cutting creatures across falling rocks; show four foot contacts and feminine silhouettes, and do not render bracketed labels.

[HEADER]
Minimal header with one thin rule; show only:
"Falling Slaughter Run"
"Leap, evade, cut, keep falling"

[BOARD]
Balanced 16:9 contact sheet with 9 near-equal 16:9 panels, clear gutters, natural P## order, and centered incomplete last row when needed.
Headers use `P## / camera angle + shot size / short beat`, no movement term; preserve aspect, count, and order.

[STYLE]
Clean monochrome 2D storyboard line sketch on white paper: sparse single-pass graphite-gray contours, simplified featureless figures, minimal construction marks, essential set geometry.
No fills, wash, hatching, shading, shadows, ambient occlusion, color, texture, 3D/clay volume, finished art, dense lines, or facial/anatomy/clothing/surface detail.

[REFERENCES]
Image A controls Suzune's build, long hair, cropped top, split wrap-skirt, right gauntlet, and single katana silhouette.

[CONTINUITY]
Suzune keeps an hourglass envelope, long hair, split skirt, right gauntlet, and one katana; Razorclaws are six-limbed walkers, Razorwings slim fliers.
Four rocks stay distinct; each creature attacks or evades, one meets each sword contact, and Suzune exits down-right toward more.

[RULES]
Only header lines and panel headers are visible; no panel text, arrows, icons, insets, extra panels, duplicates, ghost poses, or effect objects.

[BEATS]
Draw one storyboard panel per visual BEAT:
BEATS:
P01 / Very low front 3/4 FS / First Landing: Ground front three-quarter pitched up, low horizon and slab underside; Suzune's left foot fills foreground below her leg-waist line and hair/skirt, first Razorclaw lunging from upper right.
P02 / Low profile FS / First Cut: Knee-height profile with low horizon; Suzune extends right in an S-curve, katana touching the first Razorclaw below its airborne claw swipe, one edge arc attached.
P03 / Low rear 3/4 MLS / Second Contact: Knee-height rear three-quarter pitched down over the second slab top; Suzune's right foot pins one point below waist and hair cascade, first Razorwing diving from upper right.
P04 / Ground front 3/4 FS / Rising Cut: Ground front three-quarter pitched up with low horizon and rock undersides; Suzune bows upward, katana touching the banking first Razorwing as its wings turn away.
P05 / High side FS / Third Cut: Raised profile pitched down across the third slab top; Suzune's left toes pin one point below her curved silhouette, katana meeting the second Razorwing inside its S-turn.
P06 / Rear 3/4 MLS / Wall Clash: Chest-height rear three-quarter pitched down on the fourth rock's vertical plane; Suzune's right foot pins its face, leg and waist twisted, second Razorclaw clamping her katana.
P07 / Tight profile MS / Recoil Cut: Waist-height profile with narrow horizon; Suzune's shoulder and waist counter-rotate around the katana contact as the second Razorclaw's foreclaws flare away.
P08 / Low side FS / Under-Rock Cut: Low profile pitched up with a slab underside across frame top; Suzune's legs and bowed torso form one arc, katana touching the third Razorclaw lunging below.
P09 / High front 3/4 WS / Falling Pursuit: Raised front three-quarter pitched down over receding rocks; Suzune falls down-right with open hair/skirt, katana touching the third Razorwing as more creatures move ahead.

C3, C4, and C7 are separate slim cobalt Razorwings with turquoise wings, forked violet tails, and yellow eyes.

I had the chance to join the private beta of Pika Director’s Suite.

Think of it as a video agent you can use with your own Anthropic key. Starting from a simple idea, it can help plan the project, generate the necessary assets, then produce the videos with your approval at each stage. After generation, it automatically breaks the results into editable cuts, so you can refine everything more like you would in a video editor.

For the video below, I gave Pika Director’s Suite a fairly detailed plan. My character sheets and story were already prepared. It generated the environment references, then ran five separate Seedance 2.0 generations in parallel.

I did not feel the need to regenerate any of them. I only trimmed a small part from the first clip. A few moments could probably be polished further, but overall the result was surprisingly solid.

It is not shown in the screen recording below, but I also generated the background music through the suite.

Bright 2D animation layout panels: clean uniform dark-gray line art on light paper, flat pale-gray tone blocking with at most two flat values, spatially convincing perspective drawing with only anchors for pose, contact, direction, and result. Each panel is one frozen instant: one pose/state for the lead dancer, no before/after wording. Every panel shows exactly one lead dancer and one attached waist sash - never omit, duplicate, or ghost.

P04 / profile pressure / sleeve drag: waist-high side medium-wide; lead dancer leans screen right toward the platform edge, rear leg extended screen left, one sleeve block and sash tail trailing along the floor path.
P05 / overhead spiral / ring path: top-down wide; lead dancer fits inside the floor ring, one knee bent and one arm open, sash tail arcing around the lower half while attached to the waist, head near upper third.
P06 / low threshold / floor reach: knee-height low medium; lead dancer slides on one hip across the lower frame, front hand planted screen right, trailing foot and sash stretched screen left, platform edge cutting the rear horizon.
P07 / canted tension / folded line: canted medium close; lead dancer folds inward at center right, elbow crossing the featureless head, one knee pulled high, sash tail clutched near chest, tilted floor ring behind.
P08 / high breath / balance shelf: high-angle wide; lead dancer balances on one leg in the left third, opposite leg and arm extended across center, sash hanging straight from the waist, empty floor to screen right.
P09 / low impact / palm drum: floor-level close-wide; lead dancer's palm presses the floor at lower right, shoulder low and leg sweeping across upper frame, a small contact dust ring attached to the palm.
P10 / rising diagonal / sash wave: low full-body; lead dancer launches diagonally from lower left toward upper right, both feet clear of the floor, attached sash tail forming one arc behind the waist, wall low in frame.
P11 / intimate grip / silence mark: eye-level extreme close; featureless head and hand fill the right half, fingers clamp the sash end near the lower face, sleeve block framing the left edge, background simplified.

sheet_prompts:
Midjourney's new Draft Mode is fantastic for character creation.

It generates 24 low-resolution variations in a single run, making it incredibly easy to explore different character directions and quickly find designs you like.

Once you find a promising result, you can use those images directly in GPT Image 2 to generate character sheets.

You can also fix generation errors, modify outfits and accessories and change the visual medium or art style.

GPT Image 2 Character Sheet Prompt: 

Create an artistic 16:9 CHARACTER IDENTITY BOARD.

Use Image A as the subject and the visual medium. Name: Clara. Fix headphones. (just change this line as your needs.)

Soft off-white background. No environment, no logo, no watermark.

DESIGN DIRECTION:
Do not create a standard character reference sheet.
Create a cinematic identity board that feels like a high-end animation studio character study mixed with an artbook layout.

The layout should be asymmetrical, elegant and visually memorable.
Use large empty space, varied image scale and intentional imbalance.
Avoid grids, blueprint design, catalog layout and repetitive turnaround presentation.

IMPORTANT LAYOUT RULE:
Do not overlap any character images.
Every view must have clear separation and breathing room.
Keep all bodies, portraits, silhouettes and detail studies visually distinct.
No cropped faces, no hidden limbs, no stacked figures, no merged poses.

MAIN COMPOSITION:
Place one large hero full-body view slightly off-center as the visual anchor.

Around it, arrange smaller supporting studies with clean spacing:
neutral full-body view, back view, profile view, seated pose, leaning pose, crouching pose, top-down body angle, low-angle body angle, expressive portrait studies.

Each view should feel like a separate clean character study, not a frame from one scene.

IDENTITY LOCK:
Preserve strict identity consistency across all views:
same face, same facial proportions, same hairstyle, same outfit, same body proportions, same posture language, same visual personality.

USEFUL REFERENCE DETAILS:
Make the character readable for future image and video generation:
clear face shape, clear hair silhouette, clear outfit silhouette, clear body shape, clear hands, clear posture, clear expression range.

ARTISTIC SECTIONS:
Include a small silhouette study area with 2-3 simplified black character silhouettes.
Include a small expression study area with subtle emotional variations.
Include a small detail study area showing key visual features of the face, hair and outfit.

TEXT DESIGN:
Add one stylish CHARACTER ID block.
Keep it minimal, bold and art-directed.
Use only:
NAME
ROLE
CORE MOOD
VISUAL SIGNATURE

Use small handwritten-style labels only where helpful.
Subtle editorial arrows and annotation marks are allowed, but keep them minimal and elegant.

STYLE:
minimal, cinematic, premium, artbook-like, clean, expressive, useful for production.

The final image should feel like an artistic character identity board designed to help an AI model understand the character’s face, silhouette, outfit, posture and emotional range.

How do you turn a scene idea into a Prompt?

All you need to do is roughly describe what's in your head to an LLM. It doesn't have to be perfect or highly detailed. Once it understands the core idea, it can help turn it into a well-structured prompt.

In my case, I use a custom skill file that I built myself. After I provide the idea, it generates both a storyboard and video prompts for me. I then review the outputs and refine them through iteration, giving feedback like "make this shot wider," "change this action," or "move the camera here."

After a few rounds of adjustments, I usually arrive at the final result. The process is much closer to directing than writing a perfect prompt from scratch.

The Idea: Two characters face each other. Serenity fights like a Wing Chun master. She unleashes a rapid barrage of punches into Ruk's abdomen. The fight should feel highly energetic and sakuga-driven, with exaggerated action beats and dynamic choreography. Use 14 panels. The final attack should show Serenity launching high into the sky, then diving straight down at extreme speed. She lands with both feet on Ruk's head, driving him deep into the ground and burying him on impact. All other scenes should be equally creative and visually inventive. Emphasize fast pacing, flash cuts, burst cuts, sudden perspective changes, dramatic impact moments, and imaginative camera angles. Use aggressive screen direction, strong momentum shifts, dynamic framing, and escalating choreography to create a thrilling, high-energy martial arts sequence.
